Intervertebral disc transplantation in the treatment of degenerative spine disease: a preliminary study. Lancet 2007; 369: 993–9. Corneal transplantation. For reference to the use of immunosuppressants to treat graft rejection after corneal transplant see Corneal Graft Rejection, p.1502. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Hae- matopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is used in the treatment of a variety of malignancies, notably leukae- mias and lymphomas; to permit the use of very high-dose chemotherapy in the management of some solid tumours (bone marrow rescue); and to treat some other serious dis- orders affecting the bone marrow, such as aplastic anaemia and the haemoglobinopathies.1,2 HSCT may be autologous, in which case the patient’s own stem cells are harvested or allogeneic, where stem cells are harvested from a healthy donor matched as closely as pos- sible for HLA type.3,4 The haematopoietic stem cells themselves may be derived from: • bone marrow (classical bone marrow transplantation, BMT) • peripheral blood (peripheral blood stem cell transplanta- tion, PBSCT) • umbilical cord blood PBSCT is convenient as collection does not require hospi- talisation or general anaesthesia for the donor, and clinical studies have shown more rapid engraftment of neutrophils and platelets compared with BMT.2,5-7 However, alloge- neic PBSCT appears to increase the risk of graft-versus- host disease1,2,6-10 (see below). Allogeneic PBSCT was as- sociated with decreased relapse rates and improved dis- ease-free survival but similar overall survival in adults, when compared with BMT.6 However, in children, alloge- neic PBSCT was associated with higher mortality and treatment failure than BMT although relapse rates were similar; advanced disease status and use of colony-stimu- lating factor were also associated with poorer outcome.7 Use of umbilical cord blood is associated with slightly de- layed engraftment,2,11-13 and hence, perhaps, an increased risk of fatal infection,2,11 but a lower risk2,12,14 of graft-ver- sus-host disease (see below).
